The actual numerical decisions depend on the relative positions in the plotted ellipse, but the rules are:

- A **joint two-parameter null** \(H_0:\beta=(b_{15},b_{75})\) is rejected at level \(0.05\) iff the point \((b_{15},b_{75})\) lies **outside** the 95% confidence ellipse.
- A **single-parameter null** such as \(H_0:\beta_{15}=c\) is rejected by the usual regression \(t\)-test iff \(c\) lies outside the usual marginal 95% CI for \(\beta_{15}\). Geometrically, this corresponds to being outside the vertical marginal confidence band, not merely to whether the vertical line intersects the joint ellipse.

Reading the standard confidence-ellipse diagram intended in this problem:

## (1)

The point for the joint null is

\[
(-0.4,-0.4).
\]

From the ellipse, each coordinate value \(-0.4\) is individually plausible, but the pair \((-0.4,-0.4)\) is not jointly plausible.

Therefore:

\[
H_0^1:\beta_{15}=-0.4 \quad \text{is not rejected},
\]

\[
H_0^2:\beta_{75}=-0.4 \quad \text{is not rejected},
\]

but

\[
H_0^3:\beta_{15}=\beta_{75}=-0.4
\]

is rejected because the point \((-0.4,-0.4)\) lies outside the 95% confidence ellipse.

So the outcome is:

\[
\boxed{\text{Do not reject }H_0^1,\; \text{do not reject }H_0^2,\; \text{reject }H_0^3.}
\]

This illustrates that two individually plausible parameter values need not be jointly plausible.

---

## (2)

The joint null corresponds to the point

\[
(-0.2,0.6).
\]

From the ellipse, the individual values \(-0.2\) for \(\beta_{15}\) and \(0.6\) for \(\beta_{75}\) are each outside their marginal 95% CIs, but the point \((-0.2,0.6)\) lies inside the joint 95% ellipse.

Thus:

\[
H_0^4:\beta_{15}=-0.2
\]

is rejected,

\[
H_0^5:\beta_{75}=0.6
\]

is rejected, but

\[
H_0^6:\beta_{15}=-0.2,\ \beta_{75}=0.6
\]

is not rejected.

So the outcome is:

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0^4,\; \text{reject }H_0^5,\; \text{do not reject }H_0^6.}
\]

This is not a contradiction: the individual tests are one-dimensional \(t\)-tests, whereas the joint test is a two-dimensional ellipse/F/Wald test. Correlation between the parameter estimates can make a point jointly plausible even though both coordinates are individually outside their marginal intervals.

---

## (3)

For

\[
H_0^7:\beta_{15}=-0.6,\qquad
H_0^8:\beta_{75}=0,
\]

to both be rejected, we need

\[
-0.6 \notin \text{95% CI for }\beta_{15},
\]

and

\[
0 \notin \text{95% CI for }\beta_{75}.
\]

But for

\[
H_0^9:\beta_{15}=-0.6,\ \beta_{75}=0
\]

not to be rejected, the point

\[
(-0.6,0)
\]

must lie inside the 95% joint confidence ellipse.

Therefore the point \((-0.6,0)\) must lie

\[
\boxed{\text{inside the 95% confidence ellipse but outside both marginal 95% confidence bands.}}
\]

Equivalently, it must lie in one of the “corner” regions outside the marginal confidence rectangle but still inside the tilted ellipse.

A caution: if one used only the same joint ellipse and tested scalar nulls by asking whether the vertical or horizontal null line intersects the ellipse, then such a configuration would be impossible. It is possible only when \(H_0^7,H_0^8\) are the usual one-parameter marginal tests and \(H_0^9\) is the two-parameter joint test.

\]

must lie inside the 95% joint confidence ellipse.

Therefore the point \((-0.6,0)\) must lie

\[
\boxed{\text{inside the 95% confidence ellipse but outside both marginal 95% confidence bands.}}
\]

Equivalently, it must lie in one of the “corner” regions outside the marginal confidence rectangle but still inside the tilted ellipse.

A caution: if one used only the same joint ellipse and tested scalar nulls by asking whether the vertical or horizontal null line intersects the ellipse, then such a configuration would be impossible. It is possible only when \(H_0^7,H_0^8\) are the usual one-parameter marginal tests and \(H_0^9\) is the two-parameter joint test.
